newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Focus-Electrolux cleans up after closure decision.
newsitem.headline: Focus-Electrolux cleans up after closure decision.

text.p: Shares in AB Electrolux, the world's largest supplier of household appliances, soared to record levels on Friday after a tough restructuring programme was announced a day earlier.
New Chief Executive Michael Treschow stamped his mark on the white goods company with the surprise announcement of the two-year plan after just two months at the helm.

Treschow announced Electrolux would close about 25 of 150 plants and cut 12,000 staff from a workforce of 105,000 in a 2.5 billion crown ($321.3 million) programme which will be charged against second quarter earnings.

Electrolux's share price soared 64 crowns by Thursday's close after the news and nearly doubled gains on Friday when it closed at 592 crowns, up 63, after hitting an all-time high of 600 crowns during the session.
Several analysts said Electrolux, long held back by concern over its performance in the highly competitive white goods market, could go even higher.

U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers analyst Chris Heminway said he was looking at a mid-term price for Electrolux of 630 crowns and that it added Electrolux to its European strategy "recommended" list due to its restructuring plan.

The turnaround in Electrolux's share price fortunes came on the same day that its main competitor Whirlpool issued a warning that European white good sales were expected to decline again this year for the fifth year running.
Whirlpool predicted a one percent decline in white goods sales in Europe. "The environment (in Europe) is terribly negative," Whirlpool's European head Jeff Fettig told The Financial Times.

Analysts say the industry, which is characterised by mature markets, slow growth and extreme price pressure, is ripe for consolidation and reshuffle and it was high time for Electrolux to straighten out its balance sheet.
"Attention is very much going to be focused internally and that will give them a slight advantage in taking market share and therefore start the boat rocking," a Stockholm analyst said.

In the depressed European whitegoods market, the Electrolux name competes against Hotpoint which is the product of a General Electric joint venture, Merloni-owned brands Indesit and Ariston, as well as Siemens, Miele and Bosch.
"They are all doing the same thing although not as vigorously as Electrolux," said analyst Andrew Griffin from UBS.

Treschow told Reuters Financial Television in an interview that there were signs of a turnaround in the crucial U.S. market, where competition for Electrolux' Frigidaire unit with Whirlpool is at its toughest.
"We have been losing money for some years on white goods (in the U.S.) but there are some encouraging signs. I'm rather optimistic that we are getting past the time of losing money there," he said.
Some analysts said the announcement was a slap in the face for former chief executive Leis Johansson, who is now managing Swedish vehicle-maker AB Volvo.
"I think (Johansson's) talents are better used in the car industry but having said that, I think he has an awful lot to prove," one analyst said.
Electrolux said the restructuring costs levied in the second quarter would be partly offset by a capital gain of 600 million crowns from the sale of Husqvarna Sewing Machines.

Electrolux said in a statement that the restructure was designed to boost profit margins. Electrolux has set a long-term financial target to reach an operating margin of 6.5-7.0 percent by the year 2000.
In 1996, Electrolux posted a 19 percent drop in profit after financial items of 3.25 billion crowns, blaming weak European markets. ($ = 7.781 Swedish Crowns)
